name: St Cuthbert's Church, Kildale
text: Your train passes St Cuthbert's Church, Kildale, on the train's {side}. There was a church here in medieval times; the present one was built in 1868 to a design by George Fowler Jones, and inside are two old fonts, one probably from the 12th century.

name: Commondale
text: Your train passes near Commondale, on the train's {side}, a village in the North York Moors that was once a centre of brick-making. Unusually, its church is built of the local brick rather than stone.

name: Castleton castle mound
text: Your train passes near the castle mound at Castleton, on the train's {side}. A medieval castle stood on Castle Hill here, thought to have been abandoned when Danby Castle was built, and Castleton became the main market town of Upper Eskdale, with wool, cheese and cattle fairs.

name: Danby
text: Your train passes near Danby, on the train's {side}, whose name comes from the Old Norse for "village of the Danes". It is home to Danby Lodge, the North York Moors National Park Centre, which is an official Dark Sky site.

name: Duck Bridge
text: Your train passes near Duck Bridge, on the train's {side}, a single-arch packhorse bridge over the River Esk from the late 14th century. It is named after George Duck, a mason who restored it in 1717.

name: Lealholm Methodist Chapel
text: Your train passes near Lealholm's Methodist chapel, on the train's {side}, built in 1839 for the Wesleyan Methodists. The River Esk has flooded it many times, and the heights of the floods are marked by cuts in its outside walls.

name: Beggar's Bridge
text: Your train passes Beggar's Bridge, on the train's {side}, a packhorse bridge over the River Esk dated 1619. The story goes that Tom Ferris, a poor farmer's son, could not cross the flooded river to see Agnes, the squire's daughter he loved; he went to sea, made his fortune, became mayor of Hull and built the bridge.

name: St Hedda's Church, Egton Bridge
text: Your train passes St Hedda's Church, Egton Bridge, on the train's {side}, a Catholic church built in 1867 to replace one of 1790, which became the village's Catholic school. Inside, the chancel is richly decorated, with a painted and gilded altar.

name: Grosmont Tunnels
text: Your train passes near the Grosmont Tunnels, on the train's {side}. The first was finished in 1835 for the horse-drawn Whitby and Pickering Railway and replaced by a new bore beside it in the 1840s; the old one is now a footpath to the North York Moors Railway's engine sheds.

name: Ruswarp Mill
text: Your train passes Ruswarp Mill, on the train's {side}, a watermill on the River Esk built in 1752, where a mill was recorded in the Domesday Book. In floods in 1930 and 1931 the water reached its second floor, and a boat from Whitby's lifeboat station was dragged overland to rescue people from the mill offices.

name: Larpool Viaduct
text: Your train passes Larpool Viaduct, on the train's {side}: 13 brick arches built from 1882 to 1884 to carry the Scarborough and Whitby Railway over the River Esk and over the line your train is on. It was built of brick rather than iron because it is so close to the sea, and it now carries the Cinder Track, a path for walkers, cyclists and riders.

name: Mount Pleasant Mill
text: Your train passes near Mount Pleasant Mill, on the train's {side}, a tarred brick tower windmill with an onion-shaped cap, built in 1875 for the miller Edric Lansdall on top of the roundhouse of an earlier post mill.

name: 51 Fleetgate
text: Your train passes near 51 Fleetgate in Barton-upon-Humber, on the train's {side}, parts of which date from the 14th century: it is thought to be the oldest surviving house in North Lincolnshire. From 1900 it was a barber's and tobacconist's.

name: The Lincoln Castle Hotel
text: Your train passes near the Lincoln Castle Hotel, on the train's {side}, built for the Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire Railway and opened in 1851 as the Yarborough Arms, one of the first buildings in New Holland. It shares its name with the paddle steamer Lincoln Castle, which ran the Humber ferry from New Holland to Hull from 1948 to 1971.

name: All Saints' Church, Goxhill
text: Your train passes near All Saints' Church, Goxhill, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed church whose chancel dates from the 13th century and whose nave, aisles and tower are from the 14th and 15th.

name: Thornton Abbey gatehouse
text: Your train passes near the gatehouse of Thornton Abbey, on the train's {side}, the largest surviving monastic gatehouse in England. Augustinian canons came here in 1139, it became an abbey in 1148 and grew rich on the wool trade, and Henry VIII closed it in 1539.

name: Towneley Hall
text: Your train passes near Towneley Hall, on the train's {side}, home of the Towneley family from about 1200 until they sold it to Burnley Corporation in 1901. It is now Burnley's art gallery and museum, at the south end of Towneley Park.

name: Wakefield power stations
text: Your train passes near the former Wakefield power stations, on the train's {side}, on the River Calder at Agbrigg. The first opened in 1898, burning rubbish as well as coal; a second followed in the 1950s and closed in 1991.

name: Kirkthorpe
text: Your train passes Kirkthorpe, on the train's {side}, a village of less than 100 people whose name means an outlying hamlet with a church. Its Church of St Peter was built in the 14th century and rebuilt in 1875.

name: Millmoor
text: Your train passes near Millmoor, on the train's {side}, the football ground of Rotherham County from 1907 and then of Rotherham United until the 2007–08 season. It has been called the club's spiritual home.

name: York Cold War Bunker
text: Your train passes near the York Cold War Bunker, on the train's {side}, built in 1961 to monitor nuclear explosions and fallout across Yorkshire in a nuclear war. The Royal Observer Corps used it until 1991, and English Heritage opened it to visitors in 2006.

name: Northallerton Castle
text: Your train passes near the site of Northallerton Castle, on the train's {side}, a timber castle with a palisade wall, destroyed on Henry II's orders in 1178. What was left of its outline on the ground was removed when the railway was built, in the first half of the 19th century.

name: The Old Windmill, Appleton Roebuck
text: Your train passes near the Old Windmill at Appleton Roebuck, on the train's {side}, a four-storey brick tower mill built in about 1820 to grind corn, which can be seen from the East Coast Main Line. It lost its sails in the 1930s and fell into ruin, and in 2018 it was sold to be turned into a house.

name: Elmbank Hotel
text: Your train passes near the Elmbank Hotel in York, on the train's {side}, a house of about 1870 remodelled in 1898 for Sidney Leetham. Historic England says it has one of the finest and most complete surviving Art Nouveau interiors in England.

name: Doncaster Corn Exchange
text: Your train passes near Doncaster's Corn Exchange, on the train's {side}, opened in 1873 in the middle of the market hall on the Market Place. Above its entrance is a sculpture of a woman, over a large semicircular window.

name: All Saints' Church, Bolton Percy
text: Your train passes near All Saints' Church, Bolton Percy, on the train's {side}, consecrated in 1424 and built while Thomas Percy was rector. It is so large and fine that it is known locally as the "Cathedral of the Ainsty".

name: Holgate Windmill
text: Your train passes near Holgate Windmill in York, on the train's {side}, a brick tower mill built in 1770 for the miller George Waud. Restored from 2006, it was given five new sails in 2011 and in 2012 turned by the wind again for the first time since the 1930s.

name: St Bees Priory
text: Your train passes near St Bees Priory, on the train's {side}, a Benedictine priory founded on an older religious site and dedicated between 1120 and 1135. It was dissolved in 1539 and has been the parish church ever since; the name St Bees comes from St Bega.

name: St Bees School
text: Your train passes near St Bees School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1583 by Edmund Grindal, Archbishop of Canterbury, as a free grammar school for boys. It closed in 2015 and reopened in 2018.

name: Nethertown
text: Your train passes Nethertown, on the train's {side}, a small village on the Irish Sea coast. In the Second World War it had an anti-aircraft training camp, which later housed the workers building the Sellafield nuclear plant.

name: Thermal Oxide Reprocessing Plant
text: Your train passes near THORP, the Thermal Oxide Reprocessing Plant at Sellafield, on the train's {side}, which separated uranium and plutonium from spent nuclear fuel. Reprocessing ended in 2018 after earning nine billion pounds, but its store is to go on taking in spent fuel until the 2070s.

name: Grey Croft stone circle
text: Your train passes near Grey Croft stone circle, on the train's {side}, a ring of 12 stones. A tenant farmer toppled and buried all but one of them in 1820; they were found again in 1949 and put back as accurately as possible.

name: St Cuthbert's Church, Seascale
text: Your train passes near St Cuthbert's Church, Seascale, on the train's {side}, built of local red sandstone to a design of 1890 by C. J. Ferguson, replacing an "iron church" of 1881. Its organ was built in 1867 for St Bees Priory and moved here in 1897.

name: Ravenglass and Eskdale Railway
text: Your train passes near the Ravenglass and Eskdale Railway, on the train's {side}, a 15-inch-gauge line known locally as La'al Ratty, which runs seven miles from Ravenglass up Eskdale to Dalegarth, near Boot. The first railway on the route opened in 1875 to carry iron ore from mines near Boot.

name: Ravenglass Roman Bath House
text: Your train passes near the Roman bath house at Ravenglass, also known as Walls Castle, on the train's {side}. It belonged to a second-century fort and naval base, and its walls still stand four metres high: an update of Pevsner's guide calls it "an astonishing survival".

name: Silecroft
text: Your train passes near Silecroft, on the train's {side}, a village just inside the Lake District National Park. Near it is Black Combe, a fell 600 metres high standing on its own, from which on clear days you can see Ireland, Scotland, Wales and the Isle of Man.
